analysis.one_liner: Freezes nearly all new federal regulations for at least two years pending a White House review.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action in the House and died when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The RARE Act would have barred federal agencies from taking almost any rulemaking action — issuing new rules, proposing them, or even publishing notices — starting 30 days after enactment and lasting at least two years, until the White House budget office finished a review of existing rules. Narrow exceptions covered imminent health or safety threats, criminal law enforcement, and civil rights rules (with anti-discrimination rules carved out unless they rely on quotas or preferences). It also extended any statutory or court-ordered deadline tied to rulemaking by five months or the length of the freeze, whichever was later.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses facing new federal regulations — the moratorium would pause new substantive rules, proposals, and even notices for at least two years, delaying compliance costs and leaving the existing rulebook frozen while the Office of Management and Budget reviewed it.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits any federal agency from taking a regulatory rulemaking action for the length of the moratorium period, which runs from 30 days after enactment until at least two years later.

Exceptions are limited to imminent threats to health or safety, enforcement of criminal laws, and rulemaking to establish or enforce anti-discrimination rights (excluding any quota or preference), each requiring a written waiver from the OMB regulatory office.
Any statutory, regulatory, or court-ordered deadline dependent on rulemaking is extended by five months or until the end of the moratorium period, whichever is later.

Agency actions certified as repealing, narrowing, or streamlining rules are excluded from the freeze, and actions by banking regulators supervising insured depositories, credit unions, and housing enterprises are carved out as well.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost: new health, safety, environmental, and consumer protections would sit unissued for two years or more, and deadlines in court orders implementing federal rules would be pushed back, delaying fixes people are already owed.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public waiting on new protections

drawbacks.text: A blanket freeze blocks sensible rules along with burdensome ones — agencies could not even publish a notice of proposed rulemaking to start work on anything new, from workplace safety standards to consumer disclosures.
The bill extends deadlines in court orders implementing federal regulations, which can delay remedies already owed to people who won lawsuits against the government.

The emergency exception is administered entirely by one White House office (the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs at OMB), concentrating the decision over which public protections proceed during the freeze in a single political appointee.
Banking regulators are excluded from the freeze, so the industries with some of the most consequential post-crisis rulemaking pending in 2011 would have faced a different regime than everyone else.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For businesses facing compliance costs, a two-year pause is a real gain, and the OMB review would produce a public cost-benefit accounting of existing rules. But the freeze is indiscriminate: it stops rules that protect health, safety, wages, and consumers just as surely as rules businesses dislike, pushes back court-ordered remedies, and routes every exception through a single White House office. The costs fall on the public; the benefits fall mainly on regulated industries.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees in February 2011, it never received a markup or a vote in either one and expired when the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the RARE Act of 2011 on January 7, 2011, with Reps. Sue Myrick and Dan Burton as original cosponsors.
The bill was referred the same day to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee and the House Judiciary Committee.

In early February 2011 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts, Commercial and Administrative Law and the Oversight Subcommittee on Regulatory Affairs, Stimulus Oversight and Government Spending.
No further action appears in the record — no markup, no vote, no floor consideration — through the end of the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013.
The bill had five cosponsors, all Republicans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyday people kept the pipeline of new federal protections moving on its normal schedule; the industries that wanted a two-year freeze on rulemaking did not get one.

industries.industry: Regulated manufacturers, energy producers, and chemical firms
industries.note: The freeze would have paused every new substantive rule, proposal, and even public notice for at least two years, delaying compliance costs for companies facing new health, safety, and environmental requirements. The cost of that pause lands on the public, which waits for protections already in the works.

industries.industry: Banks, credit unions, and housing enterprises
industries.note: The bill carves out rulemaking by regulators supervising insured depositories, credit unions, and government-sponsored housing enterprises, so banking rules would have continued while other industries got a freeze. Banks would gain little and lose little from this particular bill.

Agencies would lose the ability to issue, propose, or even notice any new rule for the moratorium period, including work ordered by statute or the courts, with all exceptions routed through the White House budget office.
